title: 10,000 flips: do heads and tails meet?
hook: Flip long enough and heads and tails should even out. Does the gap between them shrink?

knows: a fair coin lands heads half the time
doesNotKnow: that the law of large numbers concerns proportions, not counts

misconception: The law of large numbers means the heads and tails counts get closer together as you keep flipping.
objective: The learner can explain that the heads share converges to 50% while the heads-minus-tails gap typically grows (like the square root of the number of flips), because the total grows faster than the gap.

claims.text: After n fair flips, the heads-minus-tails gap has a standard deviation of the square root of n: 100 for 10,000 flips.
claims.source: H - T is a sum of n independent +1/-1 steps, each with variance 1, so var = n and SD = sqrt(n); sqrt(10,000) = 100.

claims.text: The average size of the gap is about 2.5 after 10 flips, 8 after 100, 25 after 1,000 and 80 after 10,000.
claims.source: E|H - T| is approximately sqrt(2n/pi): 2.52, 7.98, 25.2, 79.8. Exact binomial sums: n = 10 gives 2.46; n = 10,000 gives 79.79 (computed in node).

claims.text: The heads share after 10,000 fair flips is within about 1 percentage point of 50% in 95% of runs.
claims.source: SD of the share = 0.5/sqrt(10,000) = 0.005; 1.96 x 0.005 = 0.0098, about 1 point.

claims.text: The 20 runs on the stage are seeded fair flips; their gaps averaged 2.5, 8.3, 16.3 and 86.1 after 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 flips (typical values 2.5, 8, 25 and 80), and after 10,000 flips their heads shares were between 49.0% and 50.9%.
claims.source: src/demos/probability/coin-gap-keeps-growing/model.ts, seed 1713 (the builder did not record whether the seed was tuned; treat as an illustration, not evidence). Re-run: mean |gap| 2.5 / 8.3 / 16.3 / 86.1 at 10 / 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 flips; share range at 10,000: 0.4898-0.5089. The fact-checker found over 300 other seeds a 95% range 57-107 for the 10,000-flip average (median 79), so the 16.3 at 1,000 flips is a low draw (about 2 SE below 25). The typical values are sqrt(2n/pi), claim c2. | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-13 (revision v2): Was 'The 20 runs on the stage are seeded fair flips; after 10,000 flips their gaps averaged 86 (largest 204) and every heads share was between 49.0% and 50.9%.' (reveal now quotes the stage's own readouts beside the typical values; 'every run' narrowed to 'these 20 runs') | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 4): Re-ran model.ts in node (seed 1713): mean |gap| 2.5, 8.3, 16.3, 86.1 at 10/100/1,000/10,000; share range at 10,000 = 49.0%-50.9%; sqrt(2k/pi) = 2.5, 8.0, 25.2, 79.8 (shown 2.5, 8, 25, 80). Seed disclosed as an unrecorded-tuning illustration and the reveal says twenty runs wobble; the low 1,000-flip mean (16.3) is a stated draw.

claims.text: The law of large numbers says the share of heads settles toward 50%; it says nothing that requires the counts to come together.
claims.source: W. Feller, An Introduction to Probability Theory and Its Applications, Vol. 1, 3rd ed. (1968), ch. III (fluctuations in coin tossing) and ch. X (law of large numbers).

claims.text: The dashed curves on the stage mark the typical (average) size of the gap after k fair flips, the square root of 2k/pi: 2.5 at 10 flips, 8 at 100, 25 at 1,000 and 80 at 10,000.
claims.source: For a fair-coin random walk the gap is about normal with standard deviation sqrt(k); the mean absolute value of a normal is sd x sqrt(2/pi). Same figures as c2. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Own node: sqrt(2k/pi) = 2.52, 7.98, 25.2, 79.8; Demo typical() shows 2.5, 8.0, 25, 80; dashed paths use the same formula at +/-. Exact E|S_k| (k C(k,k/2)/2^k) = 2.46, 7.96, 25.2, so 'about' holds.

recall.question: After a million fair coin flips, which is most likely?
options: Heads and tails within a few of each other, and the share very near 50%
Heads and tails hundreds apart, but the share very near 50%
recall.why: The gap typically grows like the square root of the flips (about 800 for a million), but 800 out of a million is less than 0.1%, so the share is very close to 50%.
